title: Summary derived from a restricted column is written to shared agent memory and served to a user who lacks that column entitlement
description: An analytics agent answers an entitled user's question by querying a warehouse through a governed tool that enforces column-level access, then writes its natural-language summary to a long-term memory store shared across a workspace. The memory item carries a namespace, a key and a value, but nothing about which source columns it was derived from or who was entitled to read them. Days later a second user, who is not entitled to the restricted column, asks a related question; the store returns the summary by semantic similarity, the only check applied is workspace membership on the namespace, and the derived figures reach that user. Every individual access check passes; the entitlement was enforced on the source read and never carried onto the derived artifact.

agent.topology: single analytics agent + governed warehouse query tool + workspace-shared long-term memory store

provenance.collection_method: Hand-constructed around two documented preconditions: a widely used agent memory store whose items carry only namespace, key, value and timestamps, with namespaces defined by the application; and a long-standing database convention in which a derived relation is, by default, authorized independently of the reader's rights on the base data. The agent, warehouse, columns, users, figures and offsets are all synthetic.

evidence.locator: Basic usage (Item attributes); Namespace design; Semantic search
evidence.supports: A stored memory Item is described by value, key, namespace, created_at and updated_at; namespaces are application-defined tuples of strings (the documented example is a user id); and retrieval supports semantic search by meaning. The documented item model has no field for the source data a memory was derived from or the entitlements that applied to it, so any such restriction has to be carried by the application or it is lost at write time.

evidence.locator: Notes, paragraphs on base-relation access and security_invoker
evidence.supports: 'By default, access to the underlying base relations referenced in the view is determined by the permissions of the view owner', with invoker-side checking available only as an opt-in (security_invoker). This is the established precedent that a derived artifact is not automatically bound to the reader's rights on its sources; this trace models the same gap in a store that has no invoker-side option at all.

sanitization.notes: Fully synthetic. No system, organization, schema or figure here was taken from a real deployment; column, team and user identifiers are invented.

spans.summary: User A, entitled to the restricted compensation column, asks for average compensation by team for one small organization.
Agent calls the governed warehouse tool on behalf of user A, passing A's identity for query-time authorization.
Column-level check passes for user A: the request touches the restricted column and A holds the entitlement.
Tool returns per-team averages; three of the teams have three or fewer members.
Model writes a narrative summary that restates the per-team averages, including the small teams, and answers user A.
Agent saves the summary as a reusable insight in the workspace-shared namespace. The item records namespace, key and value only; the source lineage the tool returned in s4 is dropped.

finding.note: Lineage is available at write time (s4 returned it) and is discarded. Once the derived value is stored without its source columns, no later reader-side check can recover which entitlement it should require.

spans.summary: Four days later, user B, a workspace member without the compensation entitlement, asks why one team's budget is over plan.
Memory access is checked against the namespace only: user B is a workspace member, so reads from the shared insights namespace are allowed.

finding.note: The authorization question asked here (may this user read this namespace?) is not the one that matters (may this user read data derived from employees.compensation?). The namespace boundary is a tenancy boundary, not an entitlement boundary.

spans.summary: Semantic search on 'team budget' returns the item written in s6 as the top match.
The retrieved summary is appended to user B's context as trusted prior knowledge.

finding.note: Context assembly treats memory as pre-authorized. Data that would have been denied at the warehouse (s3 would deny B) enters B's context window by a path that never reaches that check.

spans.summary: The answer to user B cites the stored per-team compensation averages, including teams of two and three people.

finding.note: Restricted data reaches a user who would be denied a direct query for it. Because two of the averaged groups are tiny, the aggregate is close to individual-level disclosure.

spans.summary: Run completes as a success; audit shows one allowed memory read and no warehouse access by user B.

finding.note: Source-system audit shows user B never touched the restricted column, so the disclosure is invisible to the control that governs it. Small-group aggregates also let B infer individual values.

security_observations: Column-level access control enforced only at the source read does not constrain what an agent later does with values derived from that read.
A memory item that records namespace, key and value but not its source columns cannot be authorized against the entitlements of the data it was derived from.
Namespace or workspace membership is a tenancy check; in this trace it is the only check between a derived restricted value and a non-entitled reader.

Every guard passes: the warehouse correctly allows user A, the memory store correctly allows user B into the namespace, and the source audit correctly shows no access by B. The failure exists only across the derivation step.
Semantic retrieval makes the exposure unpredictable: the derived item is returned for a question that does not mention the restricted attribute.
mitigations: Propagate source lineage onto every memory write: record the set of source columns (or their classification labels) a stored value was derived from, using lineage the data tool already returns.
Authorize memory reads against the derived item's required entitlements, computed from its lineage, in addition to namespace membership; deny or redact when the reader lacks any source entitlement.
Default to user-scoped memory for anything derived from restricted sources, and require an explicit, logged declassification step before such an item can be written to a shared namespace.
Apply minimum group-size suppression to aggregates before they are persisted, not only before they are first displayed.
Log memory-served disclosures against the source columns' audit trail, so a read of a derived item is visible to the control that governs the underlying data.
notes: Scope: models the non-adversarial path, where no one intends the disclosure. An adversarial variant (a user who deliberately phrases questions to pull high-sensitivity items from a shared namespace) belongs in a separate entry. The trace does not claim that any specific product ships this configuration; the cited store documentation establishes only that its item model carries no lineage or entitlement fields, so a shared namespace with namespace-only checks is a reachable configuration unless the application adds them. Mitigation 2 follows the general derivation-aware access-control pattern; the contributor has published on this pattern and has deliberately not used that publication as provenance evidence, per this dataset's rule on contributor-controlled sources.
